items.definition: Generic Tagus term for any small river-traffic or fishing boat; later differentiated by function and route.
The two main kinds of river-navigation boats serving Lisbon in the 16th century.
Shallow-water inlets of the Tagus that boats had to enter, requiring suitable hull designs.
Keel; a hull type chosen for certain boats depending on their function and route.
Half keel; an intermediate hull type between full keel and flat bottom.
Flat bottom; a hull suited to shallow waters.
Curved or straight bows, a design variation between boat types.
Masts and sail plan, which varied among boat types according to use.
Caulkers, craftsmen who helped build the wooden traditional boats.
Shipwrights who built the wooden traditional Tagus boats in riverside yards.
Shipyards, mostly in riverside towns, where the wooden boats were built, each with its own style.
A passenger-transport boat type of the Tagus.
A passenger-carrying boat type associated with Cacilhas.
A cargo-carrying boat type listed among Tagus freight boats.
A boat type used for passenger transport and for fishing.
Boat types used for fishing on the Tagus.
Elegant keelless cargo boat with a bulging hull, two prows, and a steeply raked mast; one of the Tagus's most emblematic vessels.
Lateen sail, set by the varino on a mast raked strongly backward.
Stay, a rigging line the varino set along with its lateen sail.
Decorative tuft topping the varino's pronounced, toothed forward prow.
Raised false bulwarks on the varino, helping to stow cargo better.
Hold fitted with removable floor boards or compartments for stowing cargo on the varino.
Sturdy keeled cargo vessel with open waist and flat stern, used to load and unload ships and quays; emblematic of the Tagus.
Gaff sail; the large main sail of the fragata, carried on a single mast raked aft.
One or two headsails carried forward on the fragata.
Fixed, secured rudder of the fragata.
Towing by a small rowed boat, used when no favourable wind was available for the fragata.
